paragraphs.source_en: Before he had even sat down, Meitei asked, “More ‘Giant Gravitation’?” My master replied with great solemnity, “Well, one cannot always be writing ‘Giant Gravitation.’ I am composing the epitaph for Natural Layman.” Meitei, as usual, spoke at random: “This Natural Layman of yours is a posthumous Buddhist name something like Accidental Child, I suppose.” My master asked, “Is there anyone with a posthumous name like ‘Accidental Child’?” “No, not that there is. But I imagine there might well be such a name.” My master said, “I do not think I know anyone called Accidental Child, but this Natural Layman is someone you know.” “Who on earth is he? Who has had the grand name Natural Layman bestowed on him?” “Why, Sorozaki, of course. After graduating from the university he entered graduate school and studied the subject of the theory of space; he worked too hard and finally died of peritonitis. Do not make light of Sorozaki; he was a close friend of mine.” “It is quite all right if he was your close friend; I am not saying there is anything bad about that. But whose handiwork was it to transform Brother Sorozaki into Natural Layman?” “Mine, of course. I gave him the name, because the posthumous names priests give are vulgar beyond anything.” My master was proud of Natural Layman, taking it for an exceedingly elegant name. Meitei laughed and said, “Come now, let me see this thing you call an epitaph.” So saying, he picked up the manuscript and began reading aloud: “What is this? ‘Born in space, explored space, died in space; empty, interval, Natural Layman, ah!’ Hm, it is quite good; it suits Natural Layman perfectly.” My master said happily, “Good, is it not?” Meitei teased him: “You ought to carve this epitaph on a stone used for pressing pickled radishes, toss it behind the temple hall like one of those lifting stones, and then it would be even more elegant. In that way Natural Layman would be sure to attain salvation.” My master answered with perfect seriousness, “That is just what I intend to do.” Then he added, “Excuse me, I must step out for a little while. Amuse yourself with the cat until I return.” With that, without waiting for Meitei’s answer, he drifted off.

paragraphs.source_en: Since, quite unexpectedly, I had been ordered by my master to entertain Mr. Meitei, I could hardly meet him with indifference; I meowed several times by way of goodwill and then climbed onto his knees. At this Meitei said, “Well now, you have grown quite fat!” As he spoke, he seized me by the skin at the scruff of my neck and lifted me into midair. “With his two hind legs dangling like this, I doubt this cat could catch mice. Mrs. Kushami, does this cat catch mice?” Apparently my hospitality did not satisfy him, for he began speaking to my master’s wife in the next room. From behind the paper sliding door my master’s wife replied, “Catch mice? Far from it. He ate boiled rice cakes and danced.” I had not expected my master’s wife suddenly to expose this old wound of mine. Though I was hanging in midair, I could not help feeling rather ashamed. But Meitei still would not put me down. He said, “Indeed! This cat has just the face of one who would dance. Mrs. Kushami! You must not let your guard down with a face like this; he looks exactly like a cat demon from the old illustrated storybooks.” Meitei kept talking nonsense and persistently tried to draw my master’s wife into conversation. My master’s wife, looking rather put out, laid aside the needlework in her hands and came into the parlor.
